UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                               BEFORE THE
                 FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

    Eversource Energy                             )                    Docket No. ER26-2389
    ISO New England Inc.                          )

                        REPLY PAPER HEARING BRIEF OF
                   THE NEW ENGLAND TRANSMISSION OWNERS

         The New England Transmission Owners (“NETOs”)1 respectfully submit this Reply

Paper Hearing Brief (“Reply Brief”) in accordance with the Federal Energy Regulatory

Commission’s (“FERC” or “Commission”) June 29, 2026 Order Accepting and

Suspending Tariff Revisions, and Establishing Paper Hearing Procedures,2 and in response

to the Initial Briefs filed by Opposing Parties and Trial Staff on August 28, 2026,3 in the

above-captioned proceeding.


1
 For purposes of this filing, the NETOs are: Central Maine Power Company, Eversource Energy
Service Company (on behalf of its operating company affiliates: The Connecticut Light and Power
Company, NSTAR Electric Company, and Public Service Company of New Hampshire, each of
which is doing business as Eversource Energy), Fitchburg Gas and Electric Light Company, The
Narragansett Electric Company d/b/a Rhode Island Energy, New England Power Company d/b/a
National Grid, New Hampshire Transmission, LLC, The United Illuminating Company, Unitil
Energy Systems, Inc., and Versant Power.

                                                 1
                                     INTRODUCTION

       As this Reply Brief demonstrates, the Participating Transmission Owners

Administrative Committee (“PTO AC”) has carried its burden of showing that the proposed

11.39% base return on equity (“ROE”) is just and reasonable. And neither the Opposing

Parties nor Trial Staff have demonstrated the contrary.4 Rather than identifying any defect

that would render the proposed ROE unlawful under the Federal Power Act (“FPA”), the

Opposing Parties and Trial Staff urge the Commission to adopt alternative ROEs that they

prefer based on their own alterations to the Commission’s methodology, policy

preferences, or competing interpretations of the evidentiary record. Those arguments

fundamentally misunderstand the question presented in this proceeding and Commission

precedent.

       This case arises under Section 205 of the FPA. Pursuant to that provision, the PTO

AC is required to demonstrate only that its proposed base ROE falls within the zone of just

and reasonable outcomes. It is not required to establish that its proposed ROE is the lowest

permissible ROE, the most reasonable ROE, or the only ROE the Commission could

lawfully approve. Nor does Section 205 authorize the Commission to reject a proposed

rate simply because other parties advocate a different rate that also may fall within the zone

of reasonableness. As the Commission and the courts repeatedly have recognized, multiple

 outcomes may satisfy the just and reasonable standard. Once a utility demonstrates that its

proposed rate meets that standard, the Commission’s inquiry ends.

       The PTO AC has satisfied that burden. The record demonstrates that the proposed

11.39% base ROE results from a faithful application of the Commission’s recently

reaffirmed ROE methodology as set forth in Opinion No. 594 and Opinion Nos. 569 et

seq.5 Applying that methodology to the six-month study period mandated in the Paper

Hearing Order produces a result that comfortably falls within the applicable zone of

reasonableness and reflects the returns required by investors under current capital market

conditions. Significantly, the Opposing Parties and Trial Staff do not dispute that the

NETOs’ witness Mr. McKenzie applied the Commission’s methodology to the prescribed

study period. Instead, they criticize individual inputs, advocate alternative assumptions,

and urge the Commission to revisit methodological questions that it recently resolved in

Opinion No. 594.

       Those efforts provide no basis for rejecting the PTO AC’s filing. Much of the

opposition rests on arguments that the Commission considered and rejected only months

ago. Opposing Parties seek to replace Value Line betas with Bloomberg betas, modify the

 Commission’s treatment of growth rates, alter the market risk premium calculation, change

the Commission’s weighting of long-term growth forecasts, eliminate or modify the

Commission’s size adjustment, and reshape the proxy group through subjective exclusions

that are inconsistent with the screening principles adopted in Opinion No. 594. Trial Staff

advances similar proposals.    Yet none demonstrates that the Commission’s existing

methodology does not produce a just and reasonable result or that the application of that

methodology by Mr. McKenzie here fails to yield a just and reasonable ROE. At most,

these arguments reflect a preference for alternative methodologies that merely yield lower

ROEs.

        The evidentiary record likewise confirms that current market conditions support a

materially higher ROE than the NETOs’ currently effective 9.57% base ROE. That

existing ROE was established using financial data from a study period ending in March

2013. Since then, capital market conditions have changed dramatically. Interest rates,

Treasury yields, utility bond yields, and the cost of capital generally have increased

substantially. Applying the Commission’s current methodology to contemporary data

accordingly produces a substantially higher ROE than the one derived from financial

conditions that existed more than a decade ago. The PTO AC’s proposed 11.39% ROE

reflects that reality. By contrast, many of the alternatives proposed by Opposing Parties

effectively assume that investors’ required returns have remained largely unchanged

despite profound changes in financial markets and utility investment conditions.

        The Opposing Parties’ and Trial Staff’s proposals are particularly problematic

because they do not converge around any single alternative outcome. Consumer Advocates


                                            4
 recommend a 9.00% ROE, but only as a stop gap to ROEs hundreds of basis points lower

based on approaches far removed from the Commission’s methodology.                  NECOS

recommend ROEs ranging from 9.19% to 10.21%. State Entities recommend 9.65%.

Public Systems recommend 9.79%. Acadia Center advocates approximately 9.32%. Trial

Staff recommends no more than 9.86%.             The breadth of those recommendations

underscores the central weakness in their positions. The Opposing Parties’ and Trial

Staff’s proposals do not, ultimately, indicate that the PTO AC’s proposed 11.39% ROE

falls outside the zone of reasonableness. Rather, they are the result of incorporating

differing methodological preferences among parties seeking lower outcomes. In any event,

the existence of competing ROE proposals does not establish that the PTO AC’s proposed

ROE is not just and reasonable.

       Moreover, several parties seek to reduce the NETOs’ currently effective 9.57% base

ROE, yet none attempts to satisfy the statutory findings necessary to authorize such relief.

Because this proceeding arises pursuant to Section 205, any proposal to establish a

replacement ROE below the currently effective rate necessarily requires a showing that the

NETOs’ existing 9.57% ROE is unjust and unreasonable and compliance with the

standards governing Section 206 relief. No party advocating a sub-9.57% ROE makes that

showing. That failure is especially telling given the elevated risks inherent in transmission

investment, which materially exceed those associated with state-regulated distribution

facilities. Transmission projects face lengthy siting and permitting processes, complex

environmental reviews, multi-jurisdictional approvals, public opposition, and significant

financing challenges, while the NETOs increasingly compete for capital against other


                                             5
 domestic and international investment opportunities.          These realities underscore that

proposals to reduce the NETOs’ existing ROE are unsupported both legally and

economically.

       In the sections that follow, the NETOs demonstrate that the Opposing Parties’ and

Trial Staff’s challenges either misapply the Commission’s established methodology, seek

to relitigate issues the Commission recently resolved in Opinion No. 594, or rely on

alternative approaches that may produce different results but do not establish that the PTO

AC’s proposed ROE is not just and reasonable. The Commission therefore should reject

those challenges, find that the PTO AC has satisfied its burden under Section 205, and

accept the proposed 11.39% base ROE effective November 30, 2026.

                                   REPLY ARGUMENTS

I.     The Opposing Parties and Trial Staff Have Failed to Demonstrate that the
       Proposed 11.39% ROE Is Not Just and Reasonable.

       Pursuant to Section 205 of the FPA, the filing utility bears the burden of

demonstrating that its proposed rate is just and reasonable. Once that burden is satisfied,

the Commission’s inquiry ends.6 The Commission is not permitted to determine whether

another proposed rate would be more reasonable and, even if it believes an alternative rate

would be preferable, it lacks authority under Section 205 to substitute that alternative for a

proposed rate that falls within the zone of reasonableness.7 Accordingly, the question

        The Opposing Parties’ and Trial Staff’s Initial Briefs largely ignore this fundamental

distinction. None demonstrates that the PTO AC’s proposed 11.39% base ROE falls

outside the zone of reasonableness or is otherwise unjust, unreasonable, unduly

discriminatory, or preferential. Instead, each proposes an alternative ROE that it believes

the single best ROE or the most reasonable ROE. It requires only that the PTO AC

demonstrate that the proposed ROE is a just and reasonable one.

        The Opposing Parties’ and Trial Staff’s failure to show that the proposed 11.39%

base ROE is not just and reasonable is particularly evident in their attacks on the inputs

and assumptions used in the PTO AC’s analysis. For example, much of the Opposing

Parties’ criticism focuses on the PTO AC’s use of Value Line betas in the CAPM analysis.

594 just months ago and has done so in numerous other orders.8 And none of the Opposing

Parties or Trial Staff presents an analysis demonstrating that the PTO AC’s Value Line-

based results are unreasonable. Instead, each simply substitutes Bloomberg betas for the

Value Line betas used by the PTO AC. Their collective position therefore reflects nothing

more than a preference for Bloomberg betas over Value Line betas. Such a preference is

insufficient to defeat a Section 205 filing in light of Commission precedent.

          The same flaw permeates the Opposing Parties’ and Trial Staff’s objections to other

components of the PTO AC’s analysis. Rather than demonstrating that the PTO AC’s

application of the Commission’s established methodology yields an unjust or unreasonable

ROE, they propose alternative assumptions and methodologies that they believe would

produce a lower result. But the relevant question in this Section 205 proceeding is not

whether different assumptions could produce different results. The question is whether the

PTO AC’s reliance on the methodology approved by the Commission in Opinion No. 594

produces a just and reasonable ROE.             Disagreement with the Opinion No. 594

methodology does not answer that question. Because the record demonstrates that the

proposed ROE falls within the zone of just and reasonable outcomes, the Commission

should accept the PTO AC’s proposed 11.39% base ROE.

 II.      The Opposing Parties’ Claim that the NETOs’ Cost of Equity Has Barely
         Changed Since 2012-2013 Defies Economic Reality.

         The Commission established the NETOs’ current 9.57% base ROE in Opinion No.

594 using financial data from October 2012 through March 2013 and rejected requests to

update its analysis using more recent capital market information.9 Accordingly, the

existing 9.57% ROE reflects the return the Commission determined was necessary to

attract capital under market conditions that prevailed more than a decade ago, not the

market conditions that exist today.

         In this Section 205 proceeding, the Commission directed the parties to apply its

ROE methodology using financial data from the six-month study period ending March 31,

2026.10      Mr. McKenzie’s analysis does exactly that.       Applying the Commission’s

methodology, as adopted in Opinion No. 594, to current financial data produces a base

ROE of 11.39%.11 Mr. McKenzie does not alter, adjust, or depart from the Commission’s

methodology to reach that result.        To the contrary, he applies the Commission’s

methodology used to determine the 9.57% ROE notwithstanding his criticisms of certain

          The State Entities’ analysis is also flawed because it largely ignores the

Commission’s longstanding recognition that interstate transmission investment entails

additional risks absent in state-regulated distribution operations.28 While the D.C. Circuit

vacated Opinion No. 531 on other grounds, it did not reject the Commission’s findings

return necessary to attract capital for transmission investment by the NETOs under current

market conditions.

III.     The PTO AC’s Analysis Using Value Line Betas is Unrefuted by Any Opposing
         Party.

         The PTO AC’s proposed 11.39% ROE is supported by a straightforward application

of the Commission’s CAPM methodology as adopted in Opinion No. 594.31 Applying that

methodology, Mr. McKenzie calculates a CAPM range of reasonableness of 10.57% to

13.23%, with a midpoint of 11.90%.32            In determining that range, Mr. McKenzie

conservatively applies the Commission’s natural break test to exclude Algonquin as the

high-end outlier and, if Fortis is included in the proxy group, Fortis as the low-end outlier.33
